name: Growth-plate peptides (IGF-1/MK-677 for height)

card.summary: Growth hormone secretagogues like MK-677 (and IGF-1 products) pitched as a way to gain height; trials exist only in children with growth hormone deficiency, none in healthy short people.
card.aka: MK-677, ibutamoren, LUM-201, GH secretagogues, heightmaxxing peptides
card.note: MK-677 is an unapproved investigational drug, and no trials have tested it for height in healthy short individuals.

quick.overview:
This entry covers the practice of using growth hormone (GH) boosting compounds, most often the oral drug MK-677 (ibutamoren) and sometimes IGF-1 products, in an attempt to grow taller before the growth plates close. It sits within the wider height discourse in looksmaxxing communities.

Published research on these compounds is in children and adults with diagnosed growth hormone deficiency or in older adults, not in healthy people who are simply short. Comparisons of GH treatments in deficient children measure height velocity and IGF-1 levels, and a Phase 3 trial of LUM-201 (the pharmaceutical name for ibutamoren) in children with GH deficiency is registered.
quick.mechanism: MK-677 mimics ghrelin at the ghrelin receptor and raises GH and IGF-1 levels, which are the hormones that drive growth in childhood. In growth hormone deficiency, injected GH is the standard therapy and is reported to add roughly 5 to 10 cm to predicted adult height in treated short-stature children.
quick.risks: MK-677 is an Investigational New Drug and not approved for marketing in the US. Adult studies describe raised cortisol alongside raised GH and IGF-1. No published trial tests these compounds for height in healthy people, and growth plate closure limits any growth window after puberty.

lead: Growth-plate peptides is a looksmaxxing term for the use of growth hormone (GH) secretagogues and related products, chiefly MK-677 (ibutamoren) and IGF-1, with the aim of increasing height. MK-677 is an experimental, orally active drug that stimulates the ghrelin receptor and raises GH and IGF-1 levels.[1]

Research on GH-axis drugs for height concerns children with diagnosed growth hormone deficiency. A 2026 meta-analysis compared once-weekly somatrogon with daily somatropin in prepubertal children with GH deficiency, measuring IGF-1, height SDS and height velocity.[2] A Phase 3 trial of LUM-201, the pharmaceutical name for ibutamoren, in children with GH deficiency is registered.[3] No published trial has tested these compounds for height in healthy short individuals.

Short stature is typically defined medically as adult height more than two standard deviations below the mean, and GH therapy is reported to add about 5 to 10 cm to predicted final height in treated children, at high cost.[4]
infobox: Investigational, not approved in the US[1]
Children with GH deficiency, older adults

paras: The practice centres on the idea that raising GH and IGF-1 during or near the end of puberty could lengthen long bones before the growth plates fuse. In community usage the products are grouped as peptides or secretagogues, although MK-677 is a non-peptide small molecule.[1]

Ibutamoren was developed as MK-677 (L-163,191), with early design work described in a 1995 paper, and has been associated with Merck and later Lumos Pharma. A former tentative brand name was Oratrope.[1]
Ibutamoren mimics the body's own hormone ghrelin, increasing secretion of GH and IGF-1 and keeping IGF-1 elevated for up to about 24 hours after a dose. It also raises cortisol.[1]
In adults, studies reported increases in lean body mass without changes in total fat mass, and higher bone mineral density, prompting interest in frailty in older people.[1]

No studies in healthy short people were found. Research related to this topic is limited to patients with diagnosed deficiency. In children with GH deficiency, a study reported that ibutamoren raised GH levels more than other GH secretagogues, and Phase 2 trials of LUM-201 in paediatric GH deficiency are reported to have met their endpoints.[1] A Phase 3 study of LUM-201 in 150 children with GH deficiency began in 2026.[3]

A systematic review of seven studies compared weekly somatrogon with daily somatropin in prepubertal GH-deficient children and found greater IGF-1 SDS increases with somatrogon but no significant difference in height SDS change.[2] A long-term observational study in children born small for gestational age reported that GH treatment improved height without leading to insulin resistance or excessive IGF-1 rise over about 10 years.[5]
Ibutamoren is an Investigational New Drug and has not been approved for marketing in the United States. It has been used experimentally in bodybuilding and is banned in most sports.[1]
GH therapy for short stature involves years of injections, with costs of roughly US$20,000 a year for a small child, and treatment decisions are weighed against medication risks.[4]

timeline.event: Early design work on the MK-677 compound is described in a paper.[1]
A Phase 3 trial of LUM-201 in children with GH deficiency is registered with a May 2026 start.[3]
